lead: An abstract base class is a class written as a contract only. It lists method names that every subclass must provide, and Python refuses to create an object of the class itself. It exists because related classes often share a name and a promise but not a body: every shape has an area, yet no generic shape has one formula. Without the contract, a subclass that forgets area() silently returns the parent's version and the program keeps printing wrong numbers. The tool for this in Python is the abc module. Payment gateways, plugin systems and framework code use it to force every new implementation to answer the same calls.
prereq: You need: 4.4 Inheritance for subclassing, 4.5 Method overriding and MRO for replacing a parent method, and 4.3 Encapsulation and abstraction for properties.

sections.h3: The problem: a promise with no body

blocks.text: Suppose Shape is a parent class whose area() returns 0. Circle overrides it correctly. A new class Triangle is written in a hurry and the override is forgotten. Triangle().area() returns 0, no error appears, and the grader marks the answer wrong. Nothing in the code warned the programmer that area() had to be overridden.

An abstract base class (ABC) fixes this. It is a class that states a contract: which method names a subclass must supply. Two rules come with it. First, the ABC itself cannot be instantiated, so Shape() raises a TypeError. Second, any subclass that does not implement every required method is itself abstract and also cannot be instantiated. The word abstract means "no complete implementation here", base means "subclasses build on it", and it is still an ordinary class.

The check runs when an object is created. The error appears on the line that calls Shape(), not on the line that defines the class and not at import. That timing is the whole point: a forgotten method turns into a loud failure instead of a quiet wrong answer.

Both tools come from the standard abc module, so no install is needed. ABC is a helper class that switches the check on when you inherit from it. abstractmethod is a decorator: a function that marks the method below it as required.

items: Declare the parent as class Shape(ABC):. Inheriting from ABC is what enables the check.
Put @abstractmethod immediately above each required method, for example def area(self):.
Give the body pass or raise NotImplementedError. It never runs for the ABC; it runs only if a subclass calls super().area().
Define each subclass normally, using the same method name, and write the real formula.
Create objects of the subclasses only. Calling the ABC raises TypeError.

blocks.text: Two details matter. @abstractmethod without ABC (directly or through another ABC) does nothing, because the check lives in the ABC machinery, not in the decorator. And a subclass of a subclass is checked too: the requirement travels down the chain through the method resolution order.

A property, from 4.3, is a method reached like an attribute. To make a property compulsory, stack two decorators with @property on top and @abstractmethod directly below. The order is fixed; swapping it raises an error while the class is being created.

Python has no interface keyword; Java and C# have one, Python does not. The usual substitute is a pure abstract class: every method is abstract, there is no stored data and no behaviour. Its only job is the contract, so some syllabi call these interfaces. Because Python allows multiple inheritance, one class can accept several contracts at once: class SmartKettle(Heatable, Timer) must implement both heat() and start_timer(), and the MRO decides which parent wins where real code exists. Many programmers name such classes with an -able ending: Printable, Comparable, Serializable.

figure.caption: Abstract Shape holds the required method area(); Circle with radius 2 and Rectangle with sides 3 and 4 each supply the formula, giving 12.5664 and 12 square units. Try Shape() itself and Python refuses.

spec.aria: Abstract Shape is the parent; Circle with radius 2 and Rectangle with sides 3 and 4 implement its abstract area method.

examples.question: Define an abstract class Shape with one abstract method area(). Circle(radius) implements area as pi*r*r and Rectangle(w, h) implements it as w*h. Using pi = 3.1416, create Circle(2) and Rectangle(3, 4), print both areas, then attempt to create Shape() and state what happens. Give the two areas in square units.
steps: Import the tools: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod.
Declare class Shape(ABC) and decorate area with @abstractmethod, body pass.
Circle stores radius r = 2 in __init__; area returns 3.1416 x 2 x 2 = 3.1416 x 4 = 12.5664 square units.
Rectangle stores w = 3 and h = 4; area returns 3 x 4 = 12 square units.
The line Shape() is reached; because area is still abstract in Shape, Python raises TypeError and the object is never created. The program catches it and prints 'TypeError raised'.
examples.answer: Circle area = 12.5664 square units and rectangle area = 12 square units; Shape() raises TypeError and creates no object.
examples.output:
Circle area: 12.5664
Rectangle area: 12
TypeError raised

traps: Inheriting from ABC alone blocks nothing. The class needs at least one @abstractmethod, or an abstract method inherited from a parent, before instantiation fails.
A subclass that implements four of five abstract methods is itself abstract. The TypeError appears when you create the object, not where the subclass is written, so beginners hunt in the wrong place.
An abstract property needs @property as the outer decorator and @abstractmethod just below it; the reverse order fails at class creation.
Setting self.wheels = 2 inside __init__ does not satisfy an abstract property. The abstract property still sits in the class, so the class stays abstract.
The failure is TypeError, not NotImplementedError. A body of raise NotImplementedError never runs for the ABC, because no ABC object is ever built.

quiz.q: Which module supplies ABC and @abstractmethod, and what does ABC do?
quiz.a: The standard abc module. Inheriting from ABC enables the abstract check, so objects of the class cannot be created while abstract methods remain.

quiz.q: Which exception is raised when you instantiate an abstract base class that still has an abstract method?
quiz.a: TypeError. Python refuses the call and creates no object.

quiz.q: Why does a subclass that forgets one abstract method also fail to instantiate?
quiz.a: The missing method is still marked abstract in the parent and is found through the method resolution order, so the subclass carries the same abstract status. Python only allows creation when no abstract method remains anywhere in that chain.

quiz.q: Why does @abstractmethod on its own, without inheriting from ABC, fail to stop instantiation?
quiz.a: The decorator only records that a method is abstract. The check that reads that record and refuses the call lives in the ABC machinery, which is switched on by inheriting from ABC or another ABC.

quiz.q: class Shape(ABC) has abstract methods area() and perimeter(). class Square(Shape) defines only area(). Trace what happens for Square() and for a Square2 that defines both.
quiz.a: Square() raises TypeError, because perimeter is still abstract. Square2() succeeds once perimeter is defined; area() and perimeter() then return real numbers.

quiz.q: Using pi = 3.1416, find the area printed for Circle(3) and for Rectangle(2, 5) when both subclass an abstract Shape.
quiz.a: Circle: 3.1416 x 3 x 3 = 3.1416 x 9 = 28.2744 square units. Rectangle: 2 x 5 = 10 square units.

quiz.q: A parent declares an abstract property wheels. A subclass defines __init__ that sets self.wheels = 4 and defines nothing else. Does Bike() work? Explain.
quiz.a: It fails with TypeError. The abstract property object is still a class attribute inherited from the parent; self.wheels = 4 creates an instance attribute only and never removes the class-level abstract method, so the class remains abstract. The subclass must define a property named wheels.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern Python adds typing.Protocol, which gives an interface without inheritance: any class with the right method shape is accepted, so the contract is checked structurally by type checkers rather than at runtime. The standard collections.abc module already hides many ready-made interfaces such as Iterable, Sequence and Mapping. ABC.register() lets you declare an unrelated class as a virtual subclass, which is how some libraries accept objects they did not write. Search for abc.ABC, collections.abc and Protocol when you move past the textbook.
